{"id": "92:20/q10", "question": "Why choose al-aʿlā in this wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q10/p1", "position": "It expresses absolute exaltedness, beyond a comparison with a lesser god or a merely convenient verse ending.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects the lesser-lord inference and says the superlative reaches the utmost degree, as in 87:1; she separately denies that al-aʿlā was chosen over al-ʿulā merely to rhyme. Al-Biqāʿī connects absolute height with creatures' inability to offer God anything independently."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q11", "question": "How does the phrase refer to God in the third person?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q11/p1", "position": "The two divine attributes effect a shift from first-person divine speech to third-person reference.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī identifies the rhetorical shift through 'his Lord' and 'Most High.'"}]}
{"id": "92:20/q12", "question": "What motive for giving does the verse affirm or deny?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q12/p1", "position": "The giver seeks God alone, neither repaying a human favor nor seeking human recompense, thanks or advantage.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers this from early reports; his Arabist allows expected future recompense as well as a past favor and Qatāda applies it to Abū Bakr. Rāzī says repaying an earlier favor merely settles a debt, whereas giving in answer to God's command earns reward. Al-Nasafī says the giver owes no one, and God rewards the deed. Al-Ṭabrisī, Qutb, Islahi, Kuran Yolu and Study Quran link sincere spending to purification; Islahi cites 76:9. Kuran Yolu says all blessings originate with God and rebuts the pagans' allegation of self-interest. Al-Bāqillānī sharpens sole devotion into no hope of reward or fear of punishment. Variants describe avoiding a person's benefit, ostentation, gratitude, or repayment."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q13", "question": "Does the denial of repayment exclude virtuous reciprocal kindness?", "turns_on": "Whether denying a repayable favor is mistakenly taken to make every return of kindness displeasing to God.", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q13/p1", "position": "The preceding denial can say the recipient had done the giver no favor requiring repayment.", "reasons": "Islahi reports this rendering as linguistically possible, but rejects the inference that returning kindness therefore cannot please God."}, {"id": "92:20/q13/p2", "position": "Returning kindness can itself please God; the verse praises sincere spending without expecting repayment or gratitude.", "reasons": "Islahi rejects an anti-reciprocity inference and prefers his own linguistically sound translation, which preserves the virtue of reciprocal kindness; his precise alternative wording is not in these notes."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q14", "question": "Who is the righteous giver described here?", "turns_on": "Competing occasion reports about Abū Bakr and Abū al-Daḥdāḥ, the sūra's proposed early Meccan setting, and whether the wording is confined to an individual.", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q14/p1", "position": "Abū Bakr, especially in freeing Bilāl and other persecuted believers.", "reasons": "Qatāda and the report from ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh's father identify him; Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd mention Bilāl. Ibn Kathīr says many commentators give this occasion, some claim consensus, and Abū Bakr is foremost under the general wording. Al-Bayḍāwī says the corresponding wretched one is Abū Jahl or Umayya ibn Khalaf. Al-Ālūsī says verses 17–end concern him; al-Imām appeals to this context against the rival ʿAlī claim, though al-Ālūsī calls the debate disputable."}, {"id": "92:20/q14/p2", "position": "Abū al-Daḥdāḥ, who gave the palm purchased from its owner.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ's palm account makes him the God-fearing giver and the refusing owner the opposite figure. Al-Qushayrī's version names forty palms but does not name the man. Study Quran questions this as the historical occasion if the sūra is early Meccan."}, {"id": "92:20/q14/p3", "position": "The wording applies generally to pious, generous believers, with Abū Bakr its foremost example.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr explicitly maintains the general wording despite reports about Abū Bakr. Study Quran says an early Meccan date would favor a general setting over the later palm story. Kuran Yolu says the passage honors believers like Abū Bakr."}, {"id": "92:20/q14/p4", "position": "A Shīʿī claim applies the passage to ʿAlī.", "reasons": "Al-Imām argues from the context that this claim fails; al-Ālūsī records his argument and notes it is open to dispute. The notes do not supply the claim's supporting evidence."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q15", "question": "What is reported about Bilāl's persecution and release?", "turns_on": "The reports vary on the seller, purchase price or exchange, and the accompanying conversations.", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q15/p1", "position": "Abū Bakr bought and freed Bilāl after persecution for his monotheism, prompting pagans to claim a prior favor or debt.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports Bilāl's defiling idols, subsequent torture, the Prophet's promise of rescue and notice to Abū Bakr, purchase with gold, and the pagans' allegation; Rāzī names his enslaver ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān and sale to polytheists for camels. Al-Qurṭubī reports Bilāl's cry 'One, One.' Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes Quraysh's allegation. Study Quran repeats the idols, testimony and rescue account."}, {"id": "92:20/q15/p2", "position": "In one account Abū Bakr bought Bilāl from Umayya and Ubayy ibn Khalaf for a cloak and ten uqiyyas.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī associates that account with the revelation of 92:4 and says Abū Bakr freed him for God."}, {"id": "92:20/q15/p3", "position": "In Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib's account Abū Bakr exchanged his wealthy polytheist slave Nustās for Bilāl.", "reasons": "Umayya offered Bilāl for Nustās; Abū Bakr first offered conversion and transfer of property, but Nustās refused. The pagans then alleged Bilāl had done Abū Bakr a favor."}, {"id": "92:20/q15/p4", "position": "Bilāl asked whether he was bought for service or for God's cause, and Abū Bakr answered God's cause and freed him.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī transmits the exchange as Bilāl's testimony."}, {"id": "92:20/q15/p5", "position": "The Prophet praised Abū Bakr for freeing Bilāl, and ʿUmar called Bilāl the master freed by their master.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān al-Taymī transmits through his father from ʿAlī the Prophet's prayer mentioning Abū Bakr's marriage connection, service during migration, and freeing Bilāl; ʿUmar's saying praises both men."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q16", "question": "How many persecuted people did Abū Bakr free in these reports?", "turns_on": "The reported count and the names in ʿUrwa's list.", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q16/p1", "position": "Six or seven, including Bilāl and ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayra.", "reasons": "Qatāda gives the uncertain count while stressing that Abū Bakr sought neither repayment nor thanks."}, {"id": "92:20/q16/p2", "position": "Seven, with Bilāl, ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayra, al-Nahdiyya and her daughter, and three other women.", "reasons": "ʿUrwa's lists name Dīnara or Dhanīra, Umm ʿĪsā or Umm ʿUbays, and a Banū al-Muʾammil or al-Muʾammal slave woman; the names vary between al-Ālūsī's notes."}, {"id": "92:20/q16/p3", "position": "The accounts describe Abū Bakr freeing vulnerable enslaved believers without a fixed count.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī mention Bilāl and other persecuted people; Study Quran describes weak slaves."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q17", "question": "What exchange with Abū Bakr's father is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q17/p1", "position": "Abū Quḥāfa urged him to free strong men who could defend him; Abū Bakr said he sought God's face or what is with God, and the passage was revealed.", "reasons": "The ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr report through his father gives the exchange and revelation through the promise of satisfaction; al-Ḥākim grades it sound. Al-Ālūsī also cites an Ibn Jarīr and Ibn ʿAsākir version in which Abū Bakr says he seeks only what is with God. Study Quran says he sought no defense."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q18", "question": "What is reported about the palm-tree occasion?", "turns_on": "Whether the donor is named, whether the price is an orchard or forty palms, and the feasibility of a Medinan occasion for an early Meccan sūra.", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q18/p1", "position": "Abū al-Daḥdāḥ bought an overhanging palm with his orchard or garden and gave it away after its owner refused the Prophet's offer of a palm in Paradise.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ says fallen dates reached a neighbor's children; the Prophet's initial offer was rejected. One narration calls the garden Ḥusnā and says Abū al-Daḥdāḥ gave the tree to the Prophet in return for a Paradise palm, who gave the garden to the neighbor; others say the tree went to the neighbor. The story maps the donor and owner to the sūra's opposed figures, with Paradise and Hell as their fates. Study Quran gives forty palms as the payment."}, {"id": "92:20/q18/p2", "position": "A version from Ibn ʿAbbās gives forty palms but does not name the donor.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī reports this variant, which al-Qurṭubī distinguishes from ʿAṭāʾ's named Abū al-Daḥdāḥ account."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q19", "question": "Does this verse establish a rank between Abū Bakr and ʿAlī?", "turns_on": "The subject of the passage and whether its stated motive is purer than ʿAlī's motive in 76:9–10.", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q19/p1", "position": "Al-Bāqillānī ranks Abū Bakr higher because the verse portrays devotion without hope of reward or fear of Judgment.", "reasons": "He compares this with ʿAlī's feeding for God's face alongside fear of the Day in 76:9–10; both act for God, but Abū Bakr's motive is described as purer."}, {"id": "92:20/q19/p2", "position": "Al-Imām uses the passage's context to argue Abū Bakr was the community's best.", "reasons": "His argument exclude

{"id": "92:20/q20", "question": "What reward follows the giver's sincere act?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q20/p1", "position": "God rewards the giver with Paradise and satisfaction far exceeding what was spent.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Nasafī connect seeking God with deserved divine reward; Jishumī says the full qualities earn Paradise. Al-Qurṭubī says the giver receives whatever pleases him in Paradise many times over his expenditure; the palm account likewise says Abū al-Daḥdāḥ will be satisfied on entering Paradise. Qutb says the promise is astonishing and builds suspense before it."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q21", "question": "What wider moral teaching accompanies this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q21/p1", "position": "Piety and sincere generosity, not bare affirmation, mark the saved; withholding an obligation is blameworthy miserliness.", "reasons": "Jishumī explicitly opposes the Murjiʾa on bare affirmation and defines miserliness legally as withholding an obligation; Kuran Yolu emphasizes purification and generosity, and the divine origin of all blessings."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q22", "question": "May one pause just before illā here?", "turns_on": "Whether illā here begins an independent 'but' clause or is syntactically tied to what precedes.", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q22/p1", "position": "A pause before illā is allowed when illā means 'but.'", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī explicitly gives this verse along with 6:119 and 4:157; a general grammatical view lets one pause where understood sentence components support it, though fuller meaning is preferable."}, {"id": "92:20/q22/p2", "position": "A pause between syntactically dependent elements is forbidden.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbārī lists genitive and complement, subject and predicate, conjunction and antecedent, and relative pronoun and clause as examples; the principle constrains pauses where the exception is construed dependently."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q23", "question": "How should Qurʾānic pauses be evaluated?", "turns_on": "Whether pause labels are useful judgments about syntax and meaning or inadmissible labels for Qurʾānic text.", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q23/p1", "position": "Classify pauses by completeness and quality, using grammar, recitation, interpretation and Prophetic practice.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports the majority's seven grades: complete, near-complete, deficient, good, near-good, bad and near-bad; they also consider the Prophet's stopping at verse endings."}, {"id": "92:20/q23/p2", "position": "Calling a Qurʾānic pause complete, deficient, good or bad is an innovation.", "reasons": "Abū Yūsuf reasons that the whole Qurʾān and each of its parts are complete and good."}, {"id": "92:20/q23/p3", "position": "One may stop where understood sentence components allow, ideally at the fullest meaning.", "reasons": "Some grammarians allow flexible pauses but prefer the point of complete meaning or a fitting estimate of it."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q24", "question": "How does the verse fit the sūra's contrasting portraits?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q24/p1", "position": "It completes the pious giver's portrait opposite the denier and links generosity, purification and final recompense.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the oaths of night, day and creation frame divergent efforts and fates. Corpus Coranicum sees two antitheses across verses 5–13 and 14–21, with ittaqā in verse 5 and atqā in verse 17; the final stanza reverses the saved/damned order and places warning and promise before worldly behavior. Islahi reads 15–21 as contrasting traits and reward. Kuran Yolu links the fire warning of verse 14 to the giving and protection of 17–20. Al-Qurṭubī's palm story maps ease to Paradise, hardship to Hell and death to wealth's loss. Qutb notes suspense before the promised satisfaction."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q25", "question": "What other scripture illuminates the phrase or act?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q25/p1", "position": "Other Qurʾānic and biblical texts parallel giving for God's face without human recompense.", "reasons": "Islahi cites 76:9 for giving without expecting thanks; Corpus Coranicum calls seeking God's face a biblical motif, comparing 76:9, Psalms 27:8 and 105:4, 2 Samuel 21:1 and Hosea 5:15. Al-Farrāʾ's ellipsis argument uses 2:272, as reported by al-Wāḥidī and Rāzī."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q26", "question": "What virtue is reported for reciting this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q26/p1", "position": "A report promises ample provision, relief from hardship and an easy path to its reciter.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī transmits the promise from the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "92:20/q27", "question": "What related prophetic promise is reported about Abū Bakr's spending?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:20/q27/p1", "position": "The Prophet hoped Abū Bakr would be called from every gate of Paradise.", "reasons": "The reported saying promises a call from Paradise's gates to one who spends two kinds of wealth in God's path; asked whether anyone receives every call, the Prophet names Abū Bakr as a hoped-for instance."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q01", "question": "What does waddaʿaka mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q01/p1", "position": "God did not take leave of, abandon, or cut off the Prophet; the farewell image refers especially to continued revelation and favor.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and al-Mubarrad derive it from farewell at parting; al-Rāghib and al-Ālūsī trace farewell to a traveler's prayer for safety, then leave-taking and leaving generally. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Baḥr call tawdīʿ an emphatic departure; al-Ālūsī records the objection that this would deny only emphatic abandonment and replies that emphasis may attach to the negation or answer the mockers' term (41:46). Al-Mutanabbī's line illustrates tender farewell; critics question whether that metaphor answers the mockers, while al-Ālūsī finds their speech sarcastic. Jishumī calls it a metaphor for revelation, support and favor; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares interrupted speech to a traveler leaving. Elmalılı says literal farewell cannot be ascribed to God. Biqāʿī adds that the nurturing Lord cannot part from his charge, as night cannot bid farewell to day. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes Qurʾānic forms at 33:48, 6:98, 11:6 and the sole past-tense use here."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q02", "question": "How is waddaʿaka read?", "turns_on": "Whether the dāl is doubled, and whether the light form is an independent verb or a reduction.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q02/p1", "position": "The common reading doubles the dāl, from tawdīʿ, bidding farewell.", "reasons": "The majority is cited by Māwardī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān and others; it conveys emphatic separation and is the verse's written form."}, {"id": "93:3/q02/p2", "position": "A lighter, undoubled dāl is read as wadaʿaka, meaning that God did not leave the Prophet.", "reasons": "Reported for ʿUrwa, his son Hishām, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr, ʿUmar, Anas, Abū al-ʿĀliya, Ibn Yaʿmur, Abū Ḥaywa, Abū Baḥriyya, Ibn Abī ʿAbla and Yaʿqūb; Ibn Jinnī calls it the Prophet's reading. Al-Ālūsī offers reduction of the doubled form or an independent verb, records al-Ṭībī's parallelism and a proposed echo of mockers' unusual wording, but says attested usage suffices."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q03", "question": "Was the simple verb wadaʿa current Arabic usage?", "turns_on": "Whether grammatical descriptions of disuse exclude attested poetic and Prophetic forms, or describe their rarity.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q03/p1", "position": "Eloquent speakers largely replaced the simple verb and its derivatives with taraka, treating some forms as obsolete or rare.", "reasons": "Sībawayh disallows wadaʿa; al-Mubarrad points to weak initial wāw; Naḥḥās mentions its heaviness and related hamza substitutions. Grammarians extend disuse to past, verbal nouns and participles. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites al-Jawharī's suggestion that poetic instances reflect poetic necessity, while Abū Ḥayyān maintains replacement in elevated speech."}, {"id": "93:3/q03/p2", "position": "The simple verb is attested in Arabic, although uncommon, so its reading needs no invented defense.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī cites a poem with waddaʿnā; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī cite Abū al-Aswad and another poet, including transitive usage. Al-Ālūsī adduces Prophetic sayings with wadʿ and al-Mustawfī's insistence that actual prose and verse usage outweigh a blanket grammatical ban; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes Khifāf's mawḍūʿ."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q04", "question": "Who is 'your Lord' and what does that title convey?", "turns_on": "Whether 'Lord/companion' in the surrounding reports names God or Gabriel; al-Ālūsī explicitly rejects Gabriel.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q04/p1", "position": "The Lord is God; the attached 'your' recalls His particular nurturing, care, protection and bond with Muhammad.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says He created, perfected and nurtured the Prophet; al-Ālūsī describes gradual care toward fitting perfection; Quṭb and al-Sāmarrāʾī hear intimate guardianship. Corpus Coranicum directs readers to 95:8 for the divine title."}, {"id": "93:3/q04/p2", "position": "The Lord or companion could refer to Gabriel.", "reasons": "Some inferred this from reports that Gabriel's visits ceased; al-Ālūsī dismisses it as far-fetched."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q05", "question": "What does qalā mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q05/p1", "position": "It means hated, detested or intensely rejected the Prophet.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd identifies al-qālī as a hater; Māwardī cites al-Akhṭal, Qurṭubī cites Thaʿlab's line and Imruʾ al-Qays, and others cite poetry. Qilāʾ denotes hatred; common yaqlī contrasts with Ṭayyiʾ yaqlā, with reported vowel and root variants. Al-Rāghib derives strong aversion from throwing away or roasti

{"id": "93:3/q06", "question": "Whom does the unexpressed object of qalā include?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding kāf fixes an implicit 'you' or omission deliberately widens the denial.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q06/p1", "position": "It means 'you': God did not hate Muhammad, supplied from the preceding kāf.", "reasons": "The prior direct object makes the addressee plain to al-Ṭabarī, al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, Ibn ʿĀshūr and most readers of the Study Quran. The reassurance answers mockers' claim about Muhammad."}, {"id": "93:3/q06/p2", "position": "Its open expression extends the denial to the Prophet's companions, followers and all whom he loves.", "reasons": "Rāzī connects this to the claim that one is with whom one loves; Biqāʿī and al-Ālūsī likewise hear breadth. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects this expansion as unsupported by context."}, {"id": "93:3/q06/p3", "position": "Without an object, it may say that despising anyone is alien to God's nature.", "reasons": "The Study Quran offers this generalization beside the usual supplied 'thee.'"}]}
{"id": "93:3/q07", "question": "Why is the object omitted after qalā?", "turns_on": "Whether clarity, cadence, courtesy, or expanded scope explains the ellipsis; several sources combine reasons, while Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contests sound alone and unrestricted scope.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q07/p1", "position": "The earlier kāf makes 'you' obvious, so the second object is omitted for concise Arabic expression.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Farrāʾ and Naḥḥās cite Arabic ellipsis; al-Zajjāj and al-Zamakhsharī compare 33:35, and al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr compare the later omitted objects in 93:6–8. Burhān rejects Ibn al-Shajarī's analysis as a change to third person."}, {"id": "93:3/q07/p2", "position": "The omission preserves the verse ending and its sound pattern.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Samīn, Burhān, Suyūṭī and others give this reason, sometimes alongside clarity. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects rhyme alone: Qurʾānic endings also serve meaning, and the last verse's thāʾ does not match a forced rhyme."}, {"id": "93:3/q07/p3", "position": "The omission avoids directly attaching the harsh idea of being hated to the honored Prophet.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contrasts severe qalā with farewell's lingering affection and hoped return; al-Ālūsī, al-Sāmarrāʾī and others call it courtesy. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says naming the Prophet with affectionate farewell while omitting him with hatred honors him twice and teaches respectful speech."}, {"id": "93:3/q07/p4", "position": "Leaving the object open broadens the denial to those beloved by the Prophet.", "reasons": "Rāzī, Biqāʿī and al-Ālūsī extend the assurance to companions and followers; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ finds this unsupported by context."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q08", "question": "How does this clause function as the answer to the preceding oath?", "turns_on": "Whether the negative reassurance itself answers the oath or merely sets up the next verse's promise.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q08/p1", "position": "Both negative clauses answer the oath; a negated oath answer needs no introductory lām.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and many later exegetes identify the oath response. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the missing lām; the second coordinated denial shares the syntax. Islahi says the answer states only the reassurance most needed. ʿIṣām al-Dīn proposes treating the denial as circumstantial before 93:4, but al-Ālūsī objects that the paired lāms and oath make that strained."}, {"id": "93:3/q08/p2", "position": "The denial is circumstantial, while the true promise in 93:4 supplies the oath's force.", "reasons": "ʿIṣām al-Dīn argues the better Hereafter proves the Lord would not abandon the Prophet; al-Ālūsī objects that the oath and paired lāms resist this paraphrase."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q09", "question": "What reassurance does the verse give about the pause in revelation?", "turns_on": "Whether the point is direct consolation, a pattern of testing, or evidence of revelation's external source; these are compatible explanations.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q09/p1", "position": "God has neither left nor hated the Prophet; the interruption of revelation does not end His choice, love, care or future favor.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Zayd gloss both denials; Zajjāj, Qushayrī, Jishumī, Ṭabrisī and Ibn ʿĀshūr apply them to continued revelation. Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī and Nasafī say God does not abandon one He chose or hate one He loved. Rāzī says a delay could mean only missing a preferable thing, never hatred, and serves as a meaningful honor when enemies allege it. Elmalılı distinguishes merciful respite from punitive abandonment; no human escapes divine governance (75:36). Quṭb sees a direct answer to a hurtful allegation; the Study Quran describes the ensuing favors and duties."}, {"id": "93:3/q09/p2", "position": "The Prophet's hardship and delay are part of divine training: alternating ease and difficulty test gratitude and patience, without divine indifference.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī reads day and night as necessary phases of growth; opposition and scant resources train the soul. He holds that the Prophet could worry his own mistakes angered God (94:2–3), and that revelation's timing follows wisdom; this reassurance addresses his private concern."}, {"id": "93:3/q09/p3", "position": "The pause proves the Qurʾān came from God, for the Prophet could not have withheld words he authored when he needed them.", "reasons": "Rāzī draws this inference from the painful interruption."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q10", "question": "Who was addressed by the singular 'you'?", "turns_on": "Whether singular second person marks Muhammad specifically or an exemplary generic addressee.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q10/p1", "position": "Muhammad is addressed, and his experience can exemplify divine care for listeners generally.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum prefers Muhammad while noting the general conduct rules and comparisons with 94:1–4 and 108:3. It adds that personal motifs need not be literal biographical records or mirror his private emotions."}, {"id": "93:3/q10/p2", "position": "The singular address may be generic, like the singular in the Ten Commandments.", "reasons": "Rippin proposes a nonindividual addressee; Corpus Coranicum considers Muhammad more probable."}]}

Al-Ālūsī says omissions in parallel versions do not undercut authenticity."}, {"id": "93:3/q11/p3", "position": "The interruption lasted three days.", "reasons": "Muqātil transmits this as an alternative to forty days."}, {"id": "93:3/q11/p4", "position": "The interruption lasted four days.", "reasons": "Umm Ḥafṣ's and Khawla's puppy reports say the dead animal was discovered after four days."}, {"id": "93:3/q11/p5", "position": "The interruption lasted several days, without an exact count.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and other reports say days or an unspecified time; al-Ālūsī says precise starts are hard to determine and only the Prophet could know exactly."}, {"id": "93:3/q11/p6", "position": "The interruption lasted a little more than ten days.", "reasons": "An unnamed report in al-Ālūsī gives this estimate."}, {"id": "93:3/q11/p7", "position": "The interruption lasted twelve days or nights.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj gives the count in many sources; Ibn ʿĀshūr adopts approximately twelve days for a second pause, as a merciful respite to acclimate to revelation."}, {"id": "93:3/q11/p8", "position": "The interruption lasted fifteen days or nights.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj and Wāḥidī state it; Ibn ʿAbbās or al-Kalbī give this count in numerous reports. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports roughly fifteen for the second interruption, attributing it to Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jurayj."}, {"id": "93:3/q11/p9", "position": "The interruption lasted twenty-five days.", "reasons": "Unattributed versions and Ibn ʿAbbās in Rāzī and al-Ālūsī give this count."}, {"id": "93:3/q11/p10", "position": "The interruption lasted forty days or nights.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Suddī and later transmitters give forty; Ibn ʿĀshūr treats a possible forty-day interruption as the earlier, unnoticed pause, distinct from the occasion here."}, {"id": "93:3/q11/p11", "position": "The interruption lasted fifty days.", "reasons": "The Study Quran includes fifty among the reported counts."}]}

{"id": "93:3/q15", "question": "What happened when Gabriel returned after the pause?", "turns_on": "Different reports describe the resumed visit through mutual speech, an encounter at the Kaʿba, removal of a puppy, or the vision at al-Abṭaḥ.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q15/p1", "position": "The Prophet and Gabriel expressed mutual longing; Gabriel said he was a commanded servant who descends only by God's order.", "reasons": "Muqātil says Gabriel longed even more because of Muhammad's honor with God. {"id": "93:3/q16", "question": "Could the Prophet have believed that God had rejected him?", "turns_on": "Whether reports of distress imply doubt in the prophetic mission, ordinary grief, or an anxious but wiser reading of a pause.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q16/p1", "position": "He could not believe God removed him from prophethood; any report of his saying so must be rejected or interpreted as testing Khadīja or describing appearances.", "reasons": "Rāzī's uṣūl scholars argue removal from prophecy would violate divine wisdom and the Prophet knew revelation follows benefit. {"id": "93:3/q18", "question": "How does the reassurance connect with what follows in this sūra?", "turns_on": "How broadly the Prophet's reassurance and the later commands extend to his followers.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q18/p1", "position": "Present assurance of continuing care leads to the promise of greater favor in the Hereafter and then remembered blessings and duties.", "reasons": "Rāzī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn al-Zubayr connect 93:3 to 93:4–5; Rāzī also links it to intercession for companions, followers and devotees, and to a future promise answering claims Muhammad would soon die. {"id": "93:3/q19", "question": "How does this verse fit the surrounding sūras and revelation sequence?", "turns_on": "Whether the most salient link is to the previous sūras' themes or the following sūra's parallel consolation.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q19/p1", "position": "It consoles the Prophet after the previous sūras' fear about dispositions and destiny, moving from the pious person's promise to God's favors and moral duties.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān links 92:17 with the Prophet; Ibn al-Zubayr recalls 91:8, 92:7, 92:12–13 and 93:3–5, then 93:9–10. Biqāʿī elaborates the faithful's discernment, angelic good news and light (10:64; 41:30; 8:29; 57:28; 6:122; 32:16–17) and reports the Prophet exhorting Ḥāritha and Abū Bakr to firmness."}, {"id": "93:3/q19/p2", "position": "Sūra 93 and Sūra 94 belong closely together in rehearsing God's favors and turning the Prophet toward action.", "reasons": "The Study Quran reports some considered them one sūra because Companions recited them in one prayer cycle without basmalah; it distinguishes Sūra 93's external needs and Sūra 94's spiritual relief, both recalling blessings before commands."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q20", "question": "Where does this revelation fall in the sūra's chronology?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted revelation orders and whether one counts the earlier and later pauses separately.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q20/p1", "position": "This is a Meccan sūra commonly placed eleventh, after an early pause and roughly eight intervening revelations.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says its Meccan setting is undisputed and gives the common eleventh placement after al-Fajr. He says the earlier possible forty-day pause escaped idolaters' notice."}, {"id": "93:3/q20/p2", "position": "Early Meccan rankings also place it fourth or seventh; it may be the first complete sūra revealed.", "reasons": "The Study Quran records fourth and seventh rankings and notes that others instead award the first-whole-sūra distinction to al-Fātiḥa."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q21", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the denial of abandonment?", "turns_on": "Whether the pause figures stable divine nearness, a pedagogical spiritual veil, or should be read only through the oath's sensory analogy.", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q21/p1", "position": "God did not veil the Prophet from nearness by sending him to people, nor neglect him after choosing him; the nurturing Lord does not abandon His charge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, al-Wāsiṭī and Bursawī apply the reassurance to enduring spiritual nearness and divine nurture."}, {"id": "93:3/q21/p2", "position": "The alternation of light and darkness is a temporary veil after disclosure that heightens the beloved's longing before final unveiling.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says God did not leave the Prophet in light with love but veiled Essence, nor reject him in darkness amid the cosmos without love. {"id": "93:3/q22", "question": "What broader relations between divine nearness and distance does the passage suggest?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q22/p1", "position": "Four ranks appear: obedient believers are near and loved, unbelievers distant and hated, sinful believers combine nearness and distance, and unbelievers' worship is outwardly near but rejected.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī distinguishes love, obedience, sin, rejection and outward worship in the paired denial of abandonment and hatred."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q23", "question": "What practice was attached to the descent of this sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q23/p1", "position": "The Prophet proclaimed takbīr when the sūra came; takbīr became a practice for this and following sūras.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī states both the report and its ritual consequence."}]}
{"id": "93:3/q24", "question": "What can historical reports establish about the verse's setting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q24/p1", "position": "Occasion reports are contextual clues around the revelation, not necessarily strict causal explanations or records of private emotion.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes early uncertainty and divergent accounts. {"id": "93:3/q25", "question": "How should the sūra's verse endings be described and explained?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:3/q25/p1", "position": "They are fawāṣil whose rhythm must be read with semantic need, not treated as forced sound matching or soothsayer-style sajʿ.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects a rhyme-only account of the missing kāf; the last verse ends in thāʾ without an attempted substitution, and Qurʾānic endings serve meaning as well as cadence."}]}

{"id": "93:4/q02", "question": "Why is the later state better for the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether the superior later good is principally the reward and honors of the next life or the growing success of the Prophet's earthly mission.", "positions": [{"id": "93:4/q02/p1", "position": "The Hereafter's lasting, pure gifts and the Prophet's honors there exceed the mixed, passing benefits and honors of this world.", "reasons": "Sahl/Tustarī names the greater stored station of praise and intercession than earthly prophethood and messengerhood; another Sulamī report adds the obeyed intercessor licensed to speak when others cannot. Kuran Yolu sees a reply to opponents' claim that his work would fail; Elmalılı says his later worldly life remained productive."}]}
{"id": "93:4/q03", "question": "What does the comparative khayr imply about the first life?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:4/q03/p1", "position": "The first life has good in it, although the later good is greater.", "reasons": "Elmalılı infers this from the comparative itself and says the broader later-stage reading adds continual growth in good."}]}
{"id": "93:4/q04", "question": "Why is the form khayr used?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:4/q04/p1", "position": "Frequent use shortened akhayr to khayr.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās gives frequency of usage as the cause."}]}
{"id": "93:4/q05", "question": "How do the lām and sentence opening function?", "turns_on": "Whether the lām is an oath answer, an initial emphasis particle, or part of an independently coordinated assertion; the disputed grammatical evidence is the emphatic nūn with sawfa.", "positions": [{"id": "93:4/q05/p1", "position": "The lām continues the opening oath's answer, alongside the denial of abandonment and the next promise.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn counts four sworn assertions. He says omission of an emphatic nūn is allowed when sawfa or an object intervenes and cites 3:158; Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī calls it the oath-lām and says sawfa replaces one nūn. Al-Samīn says even a proposed hidden subject would not bar the oath-answer function; the interlocutor also allows both lāms as oath-lāms."}, {"id": "93:4/q05/p2", "position": "The lām is an emphatic initial lām, with an omitted subject supplied in the following clause.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī supplies 'you' before sawfa because an oath-lām before a present verb normally takes an emphatic nūn. Al-Samīn disputes that the missing nūn rules out an oath answer; his interlocutor first identifies the lām as an initial emphatic one. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports al-Zamakhsharī's reading of both particles as lām al-ibtidāʾ."}, {"id": "93:4/q05/p3", "position": "The clause independently coordinates with the opening oath clauses and adds glad tidings after the denial.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says it is not the oath answer, and its generic definite nouns make a comprehensive closing assertion. Al-Ālūsī objects to a proposed circumstantial connection partly because of the paired lāms and oath."}]}
{"id": "93:4/q06", "question": "What does the definite form of the two nouns contribute?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite nouns generalize every later and earlier good or specify the Prophet's known earlier and later mission.", "positions": [{"id": "93:4/q06/p1", "position": "It makes the promise generic: each later or deferred good exceeds its earlier counterpart.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the general forms include continued revelation and every other good in both lives."}, {"id": "93:4/q06/p2", "position": "On the mission-stage reading, the articles refer back to known phases or replace possessives.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this from Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and others as a grammatical support for taking the beginning and end of the Prophet's mission."}]}
{"id": "93:4/q07", "question": "Whom does 'for you' cover, and why is it singled out?", "turns_on": "How far the second-person lām extends beyond the Prophet personally, given that some people do not fare better in the Hereafter.", "positions": [{"id": "93:4/q07/p1", "position": "The promise is addressed specifically to the Prophet, because it cannot truthfully be said of every companion or person.", "reasons": "Rāzī says some companions fare badly in the next life; specifying the obedient would expose sinners and hypocrites. Al-Biqāʿī likewise says upward progression is not everyone's lot. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says this sūra and al-Sharḥ address the Prophet (94:1-8)."}, {"id": "93:4/q07/p2", "position": "It contrasts the Prophet with hostile mockers, while the saved and his believing followers share afterlife good.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the first interpretation but argues exclusivity need not exclude all the saved: the Prophet's degree is higher and his praised station unique. Elmalılı says unbelievers also benefit from his worldly good and cites 14:36."}, {"id": "93:4/q07/p3", "position": "It extends to what is connected with the Prophet: his person, religion and community.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the lām as particularization and includes Islam's spread and the community's hoped-for good."}]}
